questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: Explain why courts once refused to remedy malapportioned legislatures
questions.stem: A member of the study group asks why courts once refused to order a state legislature to redistrict a badly malapportioned chamber.

options.text: Because malapportionment was treated as a political question beyond the reach of the courts.
Because the issue was not ripe for review until the legislature had acted once more.
options.misconception: misreads the early cases as a timing decision

options.text: Because a state legislature may set its own representative qualifications.
options.misconception: confuses apportionment with the power to set qualifications

options.text: Because the malapportionment arose from an agreement among the states.
options.misconception: attaches the problem to the compact clause

questions.explanation: Before the equal-population holdings, courts treated malapportionment as a political question and refused to order redistricting. Later cases established that representation must rest on equal population.
questions.hint: Ask how courts first characterized the claim.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how far a district exceeds the population standard
questions.stem: The study group calculates the size of a district: the population standard for the state calls for 50,000 residents per legislative district, and the plan gives this district 51,500 residents. By how many residents does the district exceed the standard?
questions.explanation: The district exceeds the standard by 51,500 minus 50,000, which is 1,500 residents. The equal-population standard permits only small, justified deviations, so plans must be built from accurate population figures.
questions.hint: Subtract the standard from the district's population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: State what advance federal review of voting changes required

stimulus.body: The group reviews the old procedure: when a covered jurisdiction changed its voting rules, it had to send the change to the federal government before taking effect, and the change could go ahead only if the reviewing officials raised no objection.

questions.stem: According to the revision notes, what did the preclearance procedure require before a covered jurisdiction could change its voting rules?

options.text: That the change be approved by a three-judge federal court at the outset of the process.
options.misconception: describes a judicial approval requirement that did not exist

options.text: That the change be submitted to the federal government in advance and pass without objection.
That the change be approved by a majority of the jurisdiction's board of elections.
options.misconception: confuses federal review with local board approval

options.text: That the change be published for thirty days before the jurisdiction could adopt it.
options.misconception: invents a general publication requirement

questions.explanation: Preclearance required a covered jurisdiction to submit a proposed change in advance and to wait; if the reviewing officials raised no objection within the review period, it could take effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the jurisdiction had to do first.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the coverage formula's denominator was defective
questions.stem: A student asks why the original coverage formula used total population rather than the number of voting-age citizens when it measured participation.

options.text: Because the drafters wanted to make coverage easier for states with high immigrant populations.
options.misconception: assumes the drafters deliberately favored immigrant states

options.text: Because the statute did not yet define voting age, so any population measure had to be used.
options.misconception: invents a definitional problem to explain the choice

options.text: Because counting non-citizens in the denominator understated the group's participation rate.
Because the coverage formula was designed to identify states with low voter turnout at all.
options.misconception: confuses the coverage purpose with turnout measurement

questions.explanation: The original formula divided registrants or voters by total voting-age population, so non-citizens enlarged the denominator and made participation look lower than it was. Later amendments corrected that.
questions.hint: Ask what the denominator counted and its effect.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a voting-age citizen population in a language minority
questions.stem: The study group checks a language-assistance trigger: a county has 40,000 voting-age citizens, of whom 2,400 belong to a language minority group. What percentage of the voting-age citizen population is in the language minority group?
questions.explanation: Dividing 2,400 by 40,000 gives 6 percent, above the 5 percent threshold that triggers minority language assistance, so the county must provide assistance in that language.
questions.hint: Divide the group by the voting-age citizen population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the decennial count is the basis for building districts
questions.stem: Another member of the group asks why the decennial census is the starting point for building legislative districts.

options.text: Because the census is the only count that includes economic information about households.
options.misconception: focuses on the census content rather than its population role

options.text: Because the census determines how many ballots must be printed for each precinct.
options.misconception: invents a ballot-production role for the census

options.text: Because the census determines the outcome of every election held during the decade.
options.misconception: treats the census as deciding election outcomes

options.text: Because the census supplies the population figures used to divide the state into equal-population districts.

questions.explanation: The census is the authoritative enumeration of population, and redistricting plans must be built from those figures to keep districts equal in population. A plan drawn on anything else cannot be defended.
questions.hint: Ask which figures the plan depends on.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the two routes by which a measure is referred to voters

stimulus.body: The worksheet describes a route by which the legislature itself sends a measure to the voters, and notes that a second route lets voters ask that a measure already passed by the legislature be sent back to them.

questions.stem: Which two routes does the worksheet describe?

options.text: The legislative route sends a measure to voters, and the petition route lets voters write new law directly.
options.misconception: confuses the petition route with the initiative

options.text: The legislative route refers a measure to voters, and the petition route asks voters to reject a passed measure.
Both routes require a majority of the legislature before the voters are asked to decide.
options.misconception: invents a legislative precondition for the petition route

options.text: Only the legislative route exists, and the petition route is a form of appointment rather than voting.
options.misconception: treats the petition route as an appointment process

questions.explanation: A referendum sends a question to the electorate, either because the legislature referred a measure or because voters petitioned to have a legislative measure sent to them. The petition route targets a passed law.
questions.hint: Ask which body sends the measure in each route.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: Total the number of measures that reach a state ballot
questions.stem: A revision worksheet asks the group to total the measures on a state ballot: three initiative petitions and two referendums submitted by the legislature. How many measures would go before the voters if all five reach the ballot?
questions.explanation: Adding the three initiative petitions and the two legislative referendums gives five measures. The distinction matters for procedure, since an initiative is proposed by petition and a referendum is referred by the legislature.
questions.hint: Add the two kinds of measures together.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose a recall serves in a state
questions.stem: A student asks why the recall exists at all when voters can simply wait for an official's term to end.

options.text: Because a recall removes an official early, and it also allows a legislature to be dissolved by the electorate.
Because terms in most states are so long that voters would otherwise have no chance to correct a mistake.
options.misconception: grounds the recall in term length rather than its function

options.text: Because the recall lets voters choose the replacement official without holding any new election.
options.misconception: describes the recall as a replacement mechanism

options.text: Because a recall is the only way a state legislature can be removed by the electorate.
options.misconception: invents a legislative recall of individual members

questions.explanation: A recall is a check on incumbents permitting removal before the term ends, and some states also allow a vote on dissolving the legislature. Removal triggers a replacement election.
questions.hint: Ask what the device does before a term ends.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: State the central function of a primary election
questions.stem: One student in the group asks what the purpose of a primary election is in a two-party state system.

options.text: To choose members of the state legislature, since primaries in that system elect the lawmakers directly.
options.misconception: confuses a primary with a general legislative election

options.text: To give voters a chance to test candidates before choosing the nominee in the general election.
options.misconception: misstates the primary as a test rather than a nomination

options.text: To select the party's nominee for the general election and, in some states, to pick convention delegates.
To decide which party appears on the ballot in the general election, which parties are otherwise barred.
options.misconception: describes a party-registration function of the primary

questions.explanation: A primary chooses the candidate who will represent the party in the general election, and in some states it also selects convention delegates. It is a party nomination contest, not a general election.
questions.hint: Ask who the primary is choosing and for what.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the size of a population imbalance between districts
questions.stem: A study group reads a mid-century description of a state: its largest legislative district held 900,000 residents and its smallest held 60,000. How many times larger was the most populous district than the least populous?
questions.explanation: Dividing 900,000 by 60,000 gives 15, an extreme imbalance of the kind courts once declined to remedy. The later equal-population holdings made plans like that untenable.
questions.hint: Divide the larger population by the smaller.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: State the population standard applied to legislative districts
questions.stem: The revision group works out what the population standard requires of a plan that divides a state into legislative districts.

options.text: That every district contain exactly the same number of residents as every other district.
options.misconception: treats the standard as requiring mathematical exactness

options.text: That every district contain a number of residents equal to a national average.
options.misconception: substitutes a national average for a state average

options.text: That districts be as nearly equal in population as is practicable, allowing only justified deviations.
That no district exceed the population of the smallest district by more than ten percent.
options.misconception: invents a fixed percentage tolerance rule

questions.explanation: The standard requires districts as nearly equal in population as practicable, so small deviations tied to geography are tolerated while large ones are not. Exact equality is not required.
questions.hint: Ask how equal the populations must be, and how strictly.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of the coverage formula's change on preclearance

stimulus.body: The note explains that before a covered jurisdiction could put a new voting practice into effect, it had to send the proposed practice to the federal government for review. The note also observes that once the formula that identified covered jurisdictions was struck down, the number of covered jurisdictions fell sharply.

questions.stem: According to the note, what happened to the preclearance requirement after the coverage formula was struck down?

options.text: It continued in every state, because the preclearance requirement never depended on the formula.
options.misconception: assumes preclearance was never tied to coverage

options.text: It became far less used, because far fewer jurisdictions fell within the coverage formula.
It was replaced by a requirement that states obtain preclearance for any rule change.
options.misconception: invents a universal preclearance requirement

options.text: It was extended to private employers, since their practices were added to the review list.
options.misconception: claims private firms were brought into preclearance

questions.explanation: Preclearance applied only to jurisdictions designated by the coverage formula, so when that formula was struck down and the designations lapsed, far fewer jurisdictions had to submit changes for review.
questions.hint: Ask how many jurisdictions the requirement actually reached.

questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the participation rate recorded under the original coverage formula
questions.stem: A study group works through the original coverage formula: a jurisdiction has 100,000 voting-age residents, and 45,000 of them registered or voted. What participation rate does the formula record?
questions.explanation: The original formula divided registrants and voters by total voting-age population, so it records 45 percent here. Counting non-citizens in the denominator depressed such rates and delayed coverage.
questions.hint: Divide the number who participated by the population used.

questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the language-assistance rule counts citizens
questions.stem: A student asks why the language-assistance rule of the voting-rights statute counts citizens rather than all residents.

options.text: Because only citizens vote, so counting non-citizens would overstate the size of the group.
Because the statute was written before the census counted citizens separately from residents.
options.misconception: explains the rule by a drafting-date argument

options.text: Because language assistance is funded by a levy on non-citizen residents who use transit.
options.misconception: invents a funding rationale for the citizenship count

options.text: Because the assistance rule applies to federal elections only, where the electorate is smaller.
options.misconception: misstates the scope of the assistance rule

questions.explanation: The statute measures the group and the voting-age population in citizens, because citizenship is what the franchise depends on. Counting residents would dilute the protection.
questions.hint: Ask who is entitled to vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of building a plan on faulty population figures
questions.stem: A classmate asks what happens to a redistricting plan when the census figures it was built on turn out to be wrong.

options.text: The plan is automatically void in every district, because no valid plan may use outdated numbers.
options.misconception: assumes any error voids the whole plan

options.text: The plan stays valid, because plans are judged on the intentions of the body that drew them.
options.misconception: treats plans as immune from accuracy review

options.text: The plan is automatically valid, because the legislature's choice of data is unreviewable.
options.misconception: claims legislative data choices are unreviewable

options.text: The plan must be redrawn to reflect the correct population, because equal population is a constitutional requirement.

questions.explanation: Equal population is a constitutional requirement, so a plan built on faulty population figures does not satisfy it and must be redrawn. The figures are the foundation of every district's legality.
questions.hint: Ask whether the population requirement is optional.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the legislative vote needed to refer a constitutional amendment
questions.stem: The study group reviews the steps for referring a constitutional amendment to voters: the chamber must approve the proposal by a two-thirds vote of its members. If the chamber has 100 members, how many affirmative votes are required?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 100 members is 66 and two-thirds, so 67 affirmative votes are needed to send the proposal to the electorate. The threshold applies to the legislative step, before any popular vote.
questions.hint: Take two-thirds of the number of members.

questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an initiative from a referendum
questions.stem: A member of the study group asks how an initiative differs from a referendum.

options.text: An initiative proposes a measure by petition, while a referendum approves a measure the legislature passed.
options.misconception: gets the referendum direction wrong

options.text: An initiative is decided by the legislature, while a referendum is decided by the voters.
options.misconception: reverses who decides the two measures

options.text: An initiative lets voters propose a measure by petition, while a referendum sends a question to the voters.
An initiative and a referendum are the same device, distinguished only by who collects the signatures.
options.misconception: treats the two devices as identical

questions.explanation: An initiative is a petition-driven proposal that bypasses the legislature, while a referendum sends an existing measure to the voters, either at the legislature's initiative or by petition.
questions.hint: Ask which device begins with a petition.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a successful recall of a legislator

stimulus.body: The flashcard notes that in one state voters may petition to remove a state legislator, and that if the removal succeeds a special election is then held to fill the vacancy. It also notes that the same state lets voters petition to remove the governor.

questions.stem: According to the flashcard, what follows a successful recall of a state legislator?

options.text: The legislator keeps the office but loses the right to run in the next election.
options.misconception: describes a sanction rather than removal from office

options.text: A special election is held to fill the vacancy the removal created.
The governor appoints a replacement, which the legislature confirms at its next session.
options.misconception: invents an appointment route to fill the vacancy

options.text: The state supreme court names a successor chosen from the same party.
options.misconception: invents a judicial role in choosing successors

questions.explanation: A recall removes the official rather than punishing them, so a vacancy follows and a replacement is chosen by election. Recall of a governor likewise opens the office rather than naming a successor.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the office the official leaves.

questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the votes behind a primary winner's share
questions.stem: A study group reviews the arithmetic behind a primary: 200,000 party voters cast ballots, and the winning candidate took 60 percent of them. How many votes did the winner receive?
questions.explanation: Sixty percent of 200,000 is 120,000 votes, and those votes are what make the winner the party's nominee for the general election. The primary selects that nominee, not the general election winner.
questions.hint: Find 60 percent of the votes cast.

questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: Characterize the doctrinal change in the courts' treatment of malapportionment
questions.stem: A student asks why the change in the courts' treatment of malapportionment is described as a shift away from treating the issue as political.

options.text: Because courts moved from deferring to the legislatures to deciding the equal-population claim themselves.
Because malapportionment became a federal crime once the coverage formula took effect.
options.misconception: invents a criminal prohibition on malapportionment

options.text: Because the state courts gained jurisdiction over the issue after the equal-population holdings.
options.misconception: describes a jurisdictional shift rather than a doctrinal one

options.text: Because the issue moved from the ballot to the census, where it is decided numerically.
options.misconception: describes a shift in forum that did not occur

questions.explanation: The change was doctrinal: courts stopped treating malapportionment as a political question and began enforcing the equal-population requirement, which put redistricting before the courts.
questions.hint: Ask whether the courts decided the claim or avoided it.

questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: Identify which legislature first faced the equal-population requirement
questions.stem: The revision group asks which chamber's districts were the first to be held to the equal-population requirement.

options.text: State legislative chambers, which were covered first because they drew the more distorted lines.
options.misconception: reverses the order in which the holdings came

options.text: Municipal councils, because local bodies are governed most directly by the electorate.
options.misconception: invents a local holding to fill the gap

options.text: The United States Senate, where the two members from each state always have equal populations.
options.misconception: describes the Senate as subject to the equal-population rule

options.text: Congressional districts, which were held equal in population before state legislative districts were.

questions.explanation: The congressional requirement came first, in 1964, and the same principle was then extended to state legislative districts in the following years, so a study timeline should list Congress before the states.
questions.hint: Ask which level of government was addressed first.

questions.explanation: Sixty days plus a further sixty gives 120 days of review before the change could take effect without objection. The procedure gave federal reviewers time to examine it first.

questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the coverage formula measured against
questions.stem: One student in the group asks why the coverage formula has been described as using the wrong measure of population.

options.text: Because it counted the population of the whole nation instead of the population of each state.
options.misconception: misstates the denominator as the national population

options.text: Because it counted school-age children, who cannot vote, in the participation rate.
options.misconception: misstates which ages the formula used

options.text: Because it measured participation against all residents rather than against the citizen population.
Because it relied on the population of registered voters, which is what it was meant to measure.
options.misconception: circular reasoning about the formula's purpose

questions.explanation: The formula's defect was its denominator: measuring registration and turnout against the total population, including non-citizens, understated minority participation and kept some jurisdictions out of coverage.
questions.hint: Ask what the rate was measured against.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: State when the statute's language-assistance duty is triggered

stimulus.body: The handout describes a rule: in covered jurisdictions, assistance in a minority language is required when members of that language group make up more than five percent of the voting-age citizen population, or when the group numbers more than ten thousand citizens, with a lower figure in the smallest jurisdictions.

questions.stem: Under the handout's rule, when must a covered jurisdiction provide assistance in a minority language?

options.text: Whenever any minority language is spoken in the jurisdiction, however few citizens use it.
options.misconception: drops both thresholds and requires universal assistance

options.text: When the group exceeds the specified share or headcount, subject to the exception for smaller jurisdictions.
Only when the language minority exceeds half of the voting-age citizen population of the jurisdiction.
options.misconception: replaces both triggers with a single majority threshold

options.text: Only when the state legislature declares the language a minority language by statute.
options.misconception: makes legislative designation a precondition

questions.explanation: Assistance is triggered by the group's share of the voting-age citizen population or by its number of citizens, with a lower headcount in smaller jurisdictions. The rule is fixed by statute.
questions.hint: Ask which two measures of group size the rule uses.

questions.explanation: Dividing 5,000,000 by 75,000 gives ten districts. The census figure is the population basis for the plan, and every district's size is measured against the same number.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the check a popular vote on amendments provides
questions.stem: A student asks why some states put constitutional amendments to a popular vote when the legislature itself could adopt them.

options.text: Because the electorate serves as a second approving body, checking the legislature on fundamental changes.

options.misconception: invents a legal-opinion requirement

options.text: Because amendments must be approved in at least two consecutive elections to take effect.
options.misconception: invents an election-frequency requirement

options.text: Because a popular vote is the only way a state can legally count the votes of its own citizens.
options.misconception: invents an exclusive role for popular votes

questions.learningObjective: Describe the role the electorate plays in a referred measure
questions.stem: One student in the group asks what the electorate is doing when it votes on a measure referred to it by the legislature.

options.text: It is nominating a candidate for public office, which is the function of a primary.
options.misconception: confuses a referendum with a nomination

options.text: It is ratifying a treaty, since a referred measure has the same status as a treaty.

options.text: It is choosing a plan of government for a new state, which requires a separate convention.
options.misconception: confuses a referendum with a constitutional convention

options.text: It is acting as a second legislative body, approving or rejecting the measure it was given.

questions.explanation: A referred measure puts the legislature's work before the electorate, which then approves or rejects it, much as a second chamber would. The voters are not nominating candidates or choosing a plan of government.

questions.explanation: Fifteen percent of 200,000 registered voters is exactly 30,000, and where the percentage yields fewer signatures the lower figure governs. The threshold is a fixed share of the electorate.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: Compare what a primary contributes to the election cycle
questions.stem: The revision group asks what a primary contributes that the general election does not.

options.text: It settles the election, since the winner of the primary takes the office outright.
options.misconception: describes the primary as the deciding election

options.text: It eliminates the general election, because the party nominee is the only candidate on the ballot.
options.misconception: suggests the primary replaces the general election

options.text: It chooses the party's candidate before voters choose among nominees from all parties in the general election.
It fills vacancies in office that occur between the two election cycles.

questions.explanation: A primary narrows the field to one party nominee, and the general election then decides the office among nominees of all parties. A primary neither fills a vacancy nor settles the election.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: State how courts described malapportionment claims in the earlier era

stimulus.body: The handout describes an earlier legal era in which courts repeatedly declined to order state redistricting, treating the question of how many residents a district should contain as a matter for the legislature and the electorate rather than for the courts.

questions.stem: According to the handout, what position did courts take in that earlier era?

options.text: Courts required strict equality of district population and ordered plans to be drawn accordingly.
options.misconception: describes the later rule as though it came first

options.text: Courts declined to order redistricting, treating the malapportionment claim as a political question.
Courts required only that districts be drawn by a nonpartisan commission.
options.misconception: invents a commission requirement

options.text: Courts ordered redistricting only where a county had been split by a boundary survey.
options.misconception: invents a narrow ground for ordering a redraw

questions.explanation: In the earlier era, courts consistently declined to remedy malapportionment, calling it a political question. Only later did the equal-population holdings make redistricting a matter the courts would decide.
questions.hint: Ask what courts said about deciding the claim.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a district's excess over its population quota
questions.stem: A study group checks a district's quota: the population standard gives each of 100 legislative seats 60,000 residents, and one district contains 80,000 residents. By how many residents does that district exceed its quota?
questions.explanation: The quota is 60,000 and the district holds 80,000, so it exceeds its quota by 20,000 residents. A deviation that large would draw a challenge to the equal-population requirement.
questions.hint: Subtract the quota from the district's population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: Explain the preventive purpose of advance review of voting changes
questions.stem: A student asks why the preclearance procedure was applied to changes that were not discriminatory.

options.text: Because the review screened out changes that might have a forbidden effect, not only proven discrimination.
Because the statute presumed every voting change in a covered jurisdiction was discriminatory.
options.misconception: assumes a presumption of discriminatory intent

options.text: Because discrimination could not be identified without the review of the change itself.
options.misconception: treats review as the only way to find discrimination

options.text: Because preclearance was a way for the federal government to control local election administration.
options.misconception: describes preclearance as a control device

questions.explanation: Preclearance was preventive: reviewing changes in advance let the government block a change with a forbidden discriminatory effect even without proof of intent.
questions.hint: Ask what the review was designed to prevent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of counting citizens instead of residents
questions.stem: The group asks what would follow if the coverage formula counted only voting-age citizens instead of all residents.

options.text: The states with the lowest citizen participation would be excluded from coverage entirely.
options.misconception: treats a formula change as a complete policy reversal

options.text: Nothing would change, because the two measures are identical in every jurisdiction.
options.misconception: assumes the two measures never differ

options.text: Every jurisdiction would become covered, because the threshold would be easier to meet.
options.misconception: assumes citizen counting makes coverage automatic

options.text: Some jurisdictions that had been left out would qualify for coverage, because the measured rate would be higher.

questions.explanation: Counting citizens removes non-citizens from the denominator, so measured participation rises where non-citizens are numerous, and some jurisdictions cross the threshold. That was the correction Congress made.
questions.hint: Ask how the rate changes when the denominator shrinks.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the headcount needed to reach the language-assistance threshold
questions.stem: A study group checks a language-assistance threshold: a jurisdiction has 30,000 voting-age citizens, and assistance is required once the group reaches 10,000 citizens. If 8,000 Spanish-speaking citizens vote, how many more are needed to reach that threshold?
questions.explanation: Ten thousand citizens are required and eight thousand are counted, so two thousand more are needed. The headcount is one of two triggers, alongside the share of the citizen population.
questions.hint: Subtract the count so far from the threshold.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the decennial count settles in a state
questions.stem: The group asks what a decennial count of the population is used to settle in a state that redistricts.

options.text: It settles which political party controls the legislature in the next decade.
options.misconception: claims the census decides party control

options.text: It settles the number of votes each party may cast in the next election.
options.misconception: invents a vote-allocation function for the census

options.text: It fixes the population base used to distribute seats and to draw equal-population districts.
It settles the list of candidates who may appear on the ballot for the next cycle.
options.misconception: invents a ballot-qualification role for the census

questions.explanation: The census supplies the population base for apportionment and redistricting, and for the coverage and language-assistance formulas. It determines neither party control nor candidate qualifications.
questions.hint: Ask which set of calculations the population figures feed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: Classify the routes by which a question reaches the voters

stimulus.body: The sheet lists three routes by which a question can go to the voters: the legislature may send a measure on its own, the legislature may be required to send a measure under a permanent rule, and voters may petition to have a legislative measure sent to them.

questions.stem: How should the group classify the three routes listed on the sheet?

options.text: All three are initiatives, because each begins with a measure reaching the voters directly.
options.misconception: labels every route an initiative

options.text: Two are legislative referendums, optional or required, and one is a citizen referendum by petition.
Two are citizen referendums and one is a legislative referendum, since one route needs a legislative vote.
options.misconception: counts the routes by who votes rather than who refers

options.text: One is an initiative, one is a recall, and one is a primary, because each is a direct use of the electorate.
options.misconception: confuses the routes with unrelated voting devices

questions.explanation: Whether the legislature refers a measure voluntarily or under a permanent requirement, the device is a referendum; a petition route aimed at a passed measure is a citizen referendum. Initiatives are proposals.
questions.hint: Ask who sends the measure in each route.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: Count the measures that reach the ballot by petition
questions.stem: A revision worksheet counts the measures on a state ballot: five initiative petitions and two legislative referendums. How many of the measures are proposals placed on the ballot by petition rather than referred by the legislature?
questions.explanation: The five initiative petitions are the measures that bypass the legislature, while the two referendums are questions the legislature sent to the voters. The distinction is between proposing and referring.
questions.hint: Count the measures proposed by petition.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a recall is an extra check on officeholders
questions.stem: A student asks why a recall is described as an extra check rather than an ordinary part of the electoral process.

options.text: Because it removes an incumbent early, and only where the state's constitution and laws provide for it.
Because a recall is available in every state, which makes it a routine part of every election cycle.
options.misconception: claims recalls are universal and routine

options.text: Because a recall replaces the general election in the states that offer it.
options.misconception: suggests a recall displaces the general election

options.text: Because a recall is the only way a state legislature can be dissolved by the electorate.
options.misconception: makes legislative dissolution the recall's only feature

questions.explanation: A recall exists only where a state's constitution and laws provide for it, and it removes an incumbent before the term ends. It sits outside the ordinary election cycle.
questions.hint: Ask where the device comes from and when it is used.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a party selects its nominee through a primary
questions.stem: The study group asks why a party holds a primary rather than letting its candidate emerge from a convention or a nomination contest.

options.text: Because a primary lets the party avoid any need to select a candidate at all.
options.misconception: suggests the primary eliminates the need to nominate

options.text: Because a primary is the only lawful way a party may campaign for office.
options.misconception: treats campaigning as the purpose of a primary

options.text: Because a primary awards the general election's office to the party's top vote-getter.
options.misconception: claims the primary winner takes the office directly

options.text: Because it lets party voters choose the nominee, which spreads control within the party and reduces the role of insiders.

questions.explanation: A primary moves the choice of nominee to the party's own voters, a democratic feature that can displace insiders who would otherwise pick the candidate. It does not award the office.
questions.hint: Ask who chooses the nominee under each method.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the population behind a bloc of legislative seats
questions.stem: A study group works through an old apportionment: a state of 2,000,000 residents elected 200 legislators, and 60 of those legislators came from districts holding 60 percent of the population. How many residents lived in the districts that produced those 60 seats?
questions.explanation: Sixty percent of 2,000,000 is 1,200,000 residents, and those residents were represented by only 60 of 200 lawmakers. That kind of imbalance is what the later equal-population holdings confronted.
questions.hint: Find 60 percent of the state's population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why unequal district populations are constitutionally troubling
questions.stem: One student in the group asks why a plan that gives some districts a much larger population than others is a serious problem.

options.text: Because the Constitution sets a maximum population for any single district.
options.misconception: invents a district population cap

options.text: Because large districts cost more money to administer than small ones.
options.misconception: explains the concern in administrative terms

options.text: Because it denies equal weight to each vote, which is the point of the one-person, one-vote principle.
Because it discourages candidates from running in the more populous districts.
options.misconception: invents a candidacy effect as the problem

questions.explanation: A wide population gap among districts means a vote in a smaller district counts for more, the inequity the equal-population rule targets. The concern is the weight of individual votes.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the weight of a single vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of no objection within the review period

stimulus.body: The card outlines the old review procedure: a covered jurisdiction sent a proposed change to the federal government, the reviewing officials either objected or allowed the change to take effect after the review period ran out, and only then could the jurisdiction implement the new rule.

questions.stem: According to the card, what happened when the reviewing officials raised no objection within the review period?

options.text: The change became final and the jurisdiction could implement it without further steps.
options.misconception: adds a further approval step that the procedure did not require

options.text: The change was cleared and the jurisdiction could implement it.
The change had to be resubmitted with a legislative justification for the second time.
options.misconception: invents a resubmission requirement

options.text: The change had to be published and approved by a second federal agency.
options.misconception: invents a second approving agency

questions.explanation: Silence within the review period functioned as clearance: the change could then take effect. That is what made the procedure a preclearance system rather than approval by a reviewing body.
questions.hint: Ask what the absence of an objection meant in practice.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a participation rate using citizens as the denominator
questions.stem: A study group compares two denominators: a jurisdiction has 40,000 voting-age residents, of whom 8,000 are not citizens, and 20,000 residents registered or voted. What rate does the same participation represent using citizens as the denominator?
questions.explanation: Removing non-citizens leaves 32,000 voting-age citizens, and 20,000 voters against 32,000 is 62.5 percent, well above what the total population would suggest. That gap is the formula's defect.
questions.hint: Divide the voters by the citizen population.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the language rule is written in terms of groups
questions.stem: A classmate asks why the statute's language-assistance rule is written in terms of the language of a group rather than the language of a single person.

options.text: Because the rule protects a community's ability to participate, and the group thresholds identify communities needing help.
Because individual language needs are handled by ordinary accommodation rules in the workplace.
options.misconception: invents a workplace analogy for voting assistance

options.text: Because individual voting materials are always provided in English by federal rules.
options.misconception: asserts a universal English-language voting rule

options.text: Because courts have held that individual language claims are never justiciable.
options.misconception: invents a bar on individual language claims

questions.explanation: The rule is written around groups because voting assistance works through community language networks and because statutory thresholds need measurable criteria. Individual questions are answered within that group framework.
questions.hint: Ask why a statutory threshold would be drawn by group.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why districting and the coverage formula share a data source
questions.stem: The revision group asks why redistricting plans and the coverage formula both depend on the same government count.

options.text: Because the count is the only source of information about how people travel to work.
options.misconception: invents a transportation purpose for the count

options.text: Because the count includes economic data that the courts consider when judging a plan.
options.misconception: invents an economic-data requirement for districting

options.text: Because the count determines how many poll places each county must open.
options.misconception: invents a poll-place function for the count

options.text: Because both depend on accurate population figures, which is exactly what the count supplies.

questions.explanation: Redistricting and the coverage formula both rest on population, and the decennial count is the authoritative source of that population. Sharing the same basis keeps the two calculations consistent.
questions.hint: Ask what the two calculations have in common.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the vote against a measure in a popular referendum
questions.stem: A study group checks a constitutional amendment referendum: 500,000 votes were cast and the amendment passed with 260,000. How many votes were cast against the amendment?
questions.explanation: Of the 500,000 votes cast, 260,000 supported the amendment, leaving 240,000 against. The popular vote is a separate step from the legislative approval that referred the measure.
questions.hint: Subtract the votes in favor from the total cast.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the two kinds of referendum by who places the measure on the ballot
questions.stem: A member of the group asks how a citizen referendum and a legislative referendum differ in practice.

options.text: A citizen referendum is decided by the legislature, and a legislative referendum is decided by the voters.
options.misconception: reverses who decides each referendum

options.text: A citizen referendum must be approved by the governor, and a legislative referendum need not be.
options.misconception: invents a gubernatorial role for the citizen referendum

options.text: A citizen referendum is placed on the ballot by petition, and a legislative referendum is placed there by the legislature.
A citizen referendum may only target laws, and a legislative referendum may only target constitutional amendments.
options.misconception: invents a subject-matter limit for each route

questions.explanation: The routes differ in who puts the measure on the ballot: petitions for a citizen referendum, the legislature for a legislative referendum. The subject matter each may reach is set by state law.
questions.hint: Ask who places the measure on the ballot.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a successful recall on the officeholder

stimulus.body: The note describes a western state's rule: voters may petition to recall a state legislator, and if a majority of the voters who vote on the recall approve it, the legislator is removed and a special election is set. The note adds that no recall is provided for judges.

questions.stem: According to the note, what is the effect of a successful recall of a state legislator?

options.text: The legislator is fined and barred from the next election, but keeps the office until then.
options.misconception: confuses removal with a penalty and a delayed departure

options.text: The legislator leaves office immediately and the vacancy is filled by a special election.
The legislator is replaced at once by a member appointed by the governor.
options.misconception: invents an appointment in place of an election

options.text: The legislator's votes in the legislature are discounted for the rest of the term.
options.misconception: invents a vote-discount remedy

questions.explanation: A successful recall removes the official at once, and the vacancy is filled by a special election. The note also shows the device is legislatively bounded, since judges are excluded.
questions.hint: Ask what the note says the officeholder's status becomes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the vote share of a primary winner
questions.stem: A study group examines a primary in which 30,000 votes were cast across five candidates, and the winning candidate received 12,000 votes. What percentage of the primary vote did the winner take?
questions.explanation: Twelve thousand out of 30,000 is 40 percent of the party vote, and that share is what makes the candidate the nominee. The primary selects the party standard-bearer for the general election.
questions.hint: Divide the winner's votes by the votes cast.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: Explain the political question reasoning behind the earlier refusals
questions.stem: A student asks why the earlier refusal to decide malapportionment claims is described as a political question doctrine.

options.text: Because the size of a legislature was thought to belong to representatives and voters, not to judges.
Because malapportionment cases raised questions about how the legislature was organized internally.
options.misconception: describes a procedural rather than political question

options.text: Because the Supreme Court lacked the power to hear disputes about state government structure.
options.misconception: attributes the refusal to a power limit

options.text: Because the plaintiffs in those cases had failed to exhaust their legislative remedies.
options.misconception: explains the refusal as a procedural exhaustion rule

questions.explanation: The doctrine let courts avoid issues they regarded as committed to other branches. The size of a legislature was treated as a matter for representatives and voters, until later holdings displaced that view.
questions.hint: Ask which branch the question was thought to belong to.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: State which chambers the population standard covers
questions.stem: The revision group asks how the population standard applies to the two chambers of a state legislature.

options.text: It applies only to the chamber whose members serve two-year terms.
options.misconception: ties the standard to the length of a term

options.text: It applies only to the upper chamber, because the lower chamber is directly elected.
options.misconception: assumes the standard follows the chamber elected by larger districts

options.text: It applies to neither chamber, because the state legislature may set its own internal rules.
options.misconception: assumes the standard leaves state legislatures untouched

options.text: It applies to both chambers, because each lawmaker in a state legislature represents about the same number of people.

questions.explanation: Equal population is required for state legislative districts as well as congressional ones, so both chambers must be drawn on an equal-population basis. An unrepresented chamber spreads its imbalance to the other.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule covers only one chamber.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of jurisdictions covered by preclearance
questions.stem: A study group notes that preclearance applied in the covered states and in the District of Columbia, and counts 22 covered states. How many covered jurisdictions were there in total?
questions.explanation: Adding the District of Columbia to the 22 covered states gives 23 jurisdictions, each of which had to submit changes for advance review. That was the reach of preclearance before the formula changed.
questions.hint: Add the district to the number of covered states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: Identify how the amended coverage formula improved on the original
questions.stem: A second member of the group asks how the amended coverage formula improved on the original one.

options.text: It raised the threshold for coverage so that fewer jurisdictions were covered.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of the amendment on coverage

options.text: It measured turnout at the state level rather than in individual counties and cities.
options.misconception: invents a change in the geographic unit of measurement

options.text: It used voting-age citizens rather than all residents and set a higher participation threshold.
It removed the participation requirement and relied only on population differences alone.
options.misconception: claims the amended formula dropped the participation test

questions.explanation: The amendment fixed the denominator by counting voting-age citizens and raised the participation level required, so coverage was aimed at places where citizens were underrepresented.
questions.hint: Ask what two changes the amendment made to the formula.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: State the form of the assistance a covered jurisdiction must provide

stimulus.body: The sheet notes that covered jurisdictions must provide voting assistance in the languages of qualifying minority groups, and that a group qualifies either by exceeding a share of the voting-age citizen population or by exceeding a stated number of citizens, with a lower number in the smallest jurisdictions.

questions.stem: Under the sheet's description, what must a covered jurisdiction do once a language group qualifies?

options.text: It must translate the state's entire election code into that language before the election.
options.misconception: describes a much broader translation duty

options.text: It must provide voting assistance, such as translated materials and language assistance at the polls.
It must restore the language group's right to vote in the state constitution.
options.misconception: invents a constitutional remedy requirement

options.text: It must close the polls in any district where the language group is concentrated.
options.misconception: invents a polling restriction instead of assistance

questions.explanation: The statutory duty is to provide assistance in the qualifying language, through translated materials and language help at the polls. It is a service obligation, not a restriction on voting.
questions.hint: Ask what form the assistance takes.

questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of districts produced by a population and a district size
questions.stem: A study group applies the census to a state with 1,500,000 residents and a plan dividing the state into districts of 75,000 residents each. How many districts does the plan produce?
questions.explanation: Dividing 1,500,000 by 75,000 gives twenty districts, and the plan is equal-population because every district holds the same number of residents based on the census figures.
questions.hint: Divide the population by the district size.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a mandatory referendum from an optional one
questions.stem: A student asks why a mandatory referendum is described as different from an optional one even though both send a measure to the voters.

options.text: Because in one case the legislature must refer the measure and in the other it may choose to do so.
Because a mandatory referendum is decided by a simple majority and an optional one by a two-thirds vote.
options.misconception: invents a vote-threshold distinction

options.text: Because a mandatory referendum covers only constitutional amendments while an optional one covers any bill.
options.misconception: confuses the trigger with the subject matter

options.text: Because a mandatory referendum is held in even years and an optional one in odd years.
options.misconception: invents a biennial trigger distinction

questions.explanation: The difference is in the legislature's duty: under a mandatory rule it must refer the measure, while under an optional rule it may do so. The vote threshold and the schedule are set separately.
questions.hint: Ask whether the legislature has a choice in each case.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: State what signing an initiative petition requests
questions.stem: A participant asks what a voter is doing when signing an initiative petition.

options.text: Approving a law that the legislature has already passed and asking for a second vote.
options.misconception: confuses petitioning with approving a measure

options.text: Calling a special session of the legislature to review the measure again.
options.misconception: invents a legislative session as the object of a petition

options.text: Removing an official from office, which is the purpose of a recall petition.
options.misconception: confuses an initiative petition with a recall petition

options.text: Requesting that a measure be drafted and placed on the ballot for the voters to decide.

questions.explanation: An initiative petition requests that a measure be drafted and placed on the ballot for the voters to decide. It proposes rather than approves, and it does not remove officials or summon the legislature.
questions.hint: Ask what the signature is asking to happen.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the votes against a recall measure
questions.stem: A study group checks a recall vote: 120,000 votes were cast, 60,000 voted to recall the official, and a majority of those voting was required. How many votes were cast against the recall measure?
questions.explanation: Of the 120,000 votes cast, 60,000 supported the recall and 60,000 opposed it, so the measure fell one vote short of the majority required. Recalls need more than half of those who vote.
questions.hint: Subtract the votes in favour from the votes cast.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an uncontested primary race
questions.stem: The study group asks what would happen to a primary that drew only one candidate in a contested race.

options.text: The primary would be cancelled automatically, because a primary needs a contest to be valid.
options.misconception: invents an automatic cancellation rule

options.text: The candidate would be elected without opposition, because no one else qualified to vote.
options.misconception: misdescribes who qualifies to vote in a primary

options.text: The race would be settled without a general election for that office, because the nomination is uncontested.
options.misconception: suggests the general election disappears from the ballot

options.text: The party would have to hold a second primary, because a single candidate cannot win a majority.
options.misconception: invents a second-primary requirement

questions.explanation: A primary nominates the party's candidate; if only one qualified, the nomination is settled without a contest, and the general election pits that nominee against other parties' nominees.
questions.hint: Ask what a primary decides.
